question: Why is problem-solving such an everyday skill for a nurse on the ward?

options.A: Shifting patient conditions and unexpected complications
options.B: Completing routine administrative chores on schedule
options.C: Performing yearly performance appraisals for staff
options.D: Writing extensive daily reports for hospital management

explanation: Patients can change in a split second! Knowing how to think on your feet when unexpected things happen is a huge part of keeping your patients safe. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h1)

question: Why do nurses need to look beyond just memorizing facts for exams?

options.A: To pass annual nursing council licensing examinations easily
options.B: To connect varying clinical signs with underlying physiological problems
options.C: To finish medication rounds within the designated time frame
options.D: To memorize more hospital policies and administrative guidelines

explanation: Exams are great, but real patients don't read textbooks! You need to connect what you see on the outside to what's happening inside the body. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h1)

question: In which phase of the nursing process do you set clear, measurable goals for your patient?
explanation: Spot on! The planning phase is where you map out your game plan and set clear goals to help your patient get better. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h2)

question: What is the main goal of the evaluation step in patient care?

options.A: Administering prescribed medications during the morning shift
options.B: Gathering initial vital signs and health history data
options.C: Writing down the final medical diagnosis from the doctor
options.D: Determining if the established patient goals were actually met

explanation: Evaluation is just checking your homework! Did our nursing care actually work? Let's check if the patient reached their goals. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h2)

question: What does thinking critically really mean for a nurse?

options.A: Rely strictly on gut feeling rather than patient data
options.B: Follow strict hospital protocols without asking any questions
options.C: Question assumptions and weigh available clinical evidence
options.D: Delegate all complex decision-making tasks to senior doctors

explanation: Critical thinking means not just accepting things at face value. You look at the evidence and ask smart questions to give the best care. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h3)

question: If a patient who just had surgery is suddenly restless and has a fast heart rate, what should you suspect?

options.A: Potential internal bleeding or an underlying pulmonary embolism
options.B: Normal recovery after anesthesia wearing off completely
options.C: A simple case of mild boredom from being in bed
options.D: Temporary hunger due to missed hospital meals

explanation: Restlessness paired with a racing heart is a classic red flag. Always stay alert for serious issues like bleeding or blood clots! [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h3)

question: What is the main goal of doing a root cause analysis after an incident?

options.A: Testing various treatment options until one works successfully
options.B: Generating multiple quick ideas during a sudden staff shortage
options.C: Finding the underlying systemic failure that caused an error
options.D: Following a branched flowchart for cardiac life support

explanation: Instead of just blaming a person, a root cause analysis digs deep to fix the actual system flaw so the mistake never happens again. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h4)

question: When is it actually okay to use trial and error in clinical care?

options.A: When deciding the correct dosage for high-risk cardiac drugs
options.B: When adjusting non-harmful variables like minor IV flow rates
options.C: When performing major emergency surgery in the theater
options.D: When diagnosing a complex life-threatening neurological condition

explanation: Trial and error has its place, but only for low-risk tweaks where a mistake won't harm the patient. Never guess with major drugs or surgeries! [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h4)

question: Which of these is an internal mental barrier that can mess with your problem-solving on duty?

options.A: Fatigue and heavy workloads narrowing cognitive bandwidth
options.B: A shortage of essential drugs in the hospital pharmacy
options.C: Lack of support from the hospital administrative board
options.D: Broken equipment in the emergency treatment room

explanation: We've all been there—when you're exhausted and overworked, it's so much harder to think clearly and solve problems quickly. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h5)

question: How does the old saying 'we have always done it this way' impact patient care?

options.A: It stifles innovation and prevents the adoption of better practices
options.B: It ensures that clinical routines remain completely safe and error-free
options.C: It encourages nurses to rely more heavily on evidence-based research
options.D: It speeds up the handover process during morning shift changes

explanation: Sticking to tradition just because 'it's how we've always done it' stops us from using modern, safer, evidence-based nursing care. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h5)

question: What is the true value of taking time for reflective practice?

options.A: Punishing colleagues who make mistakes during night shifts
options.B: Transforming clinical experiences into lifelong professional wisdom
options.C: Completing annual financial audits for the hospital ward
options.D: Fulfilling mandatory administrative paperwork for hospital licensing

explanation: Reflection turns everyday shifts into learning moments. Every tough day makes you a wiser, more skilled nurse! [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h6)

question: A nurse walks away from a tough shift asking, 'What could I have done differently during that code?' What is this called?
explanation: You got it! Looking back at your actions to learn and grow for next time is what reflective practice is all about. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h6)
